text:
Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

text:
WHEN A CREATOR SPEAKS UP, DOES HER VOICE BECOME THE TARGET? DIGITAL CENSORSHIP, META RESTRICTIONS AND THE RIGHT TO BE HEARD

A creator behind @the.ranting.gola has shared a disturbing account of restrictions on her Facebook activity. In her video, she says she cannot go LIVE for a year, send messages, post videos to her broadcast group or share videos to her Story. She also describes monetisation being unavailable and some content becoming inaccessible in India.

She says she had made a video supporting Neha Singh Rathore and opposing ABVP-related groups. According to her account, she was not clearly informed which specific post had triggered the restrictions and had to investigate the matter herself.

These are the creator’s allegations and account of her experience. The precise reason for the restrictions, the applicable Meta policy and whether a government direction was involved have not been independently established from this video alone.

But her experience raises a fundamental democratic question: What happens when ordinary citizens and independent creators lose their ability to communicate with their audiences without receiving a clear explanation?

THIS IS NOT AN ISOLATED CONCERN

Recent reporting in India makes these questions particularly urgent.

• ThePrint, 19 October 2026: Reported on a MeitY advisory asking Meta to review its Facebook and Instagram recommendation systems, alongside restrictions affecting posts and accounts connected with protests and political events.

https://t.co/QeWUIIrGmC

• Alt News, 15 October 2026: Documented restrictions affecting journalists and media organisations covering the Delhi protests, including cases in which Meta notices cited automated enforcement or government and law-enforcement requests.

https://t.co/1RjkoJX1nE

• Reporters Without Borders: Reported a broader rise in restrictions affecting journalistic content in India during 2026, raising concerns about opaque takedown processes and the public’s right to information.

https://t.co/g6FhmAUglC

These reports provide important context. They do not, by themselves, establish that this particular creator was restricted at the government's request. That question deserves a direct, evidence-based answer.

THE REAL ISSUE: TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY

Social media companies have the right to enforce legitimate community standards. But enforcement must be proportionate, transparent and open to meaningful appeal.

If a creator is prohibited from going LIVE for an entire year, the platform should explain:

Which specific post, video or action triggered the restriction?
Which rule was allegedly violated, and what evidence supports that decision?
Was the action taken under Meta's own policies, an automated system or a government/legal request?
Why were such extensive restrictions imposed, and what appeal and restoration mechanisms are available?

A vague account-status notification is not an adequate substitute for a meaningful explanation.

DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY ELECTIONS

Democracy also depends on the freedom to question power, criticise political organisations, support dissenting voices and share information without arbitrary punishment.

When restrictions disproportionately affect people discussing political controversies, the public deserves to know whether the cause is legitimate policy enforcement, automated error, coordinated reporting or an external legal direction. These possibilities must be investigated rather than assumed.

Our demand is simple: transparency from Meta, accountability from any authority that seeks unlawful restrictions, and equal protection for every citizen's right to express a political opinion.

No creator should have to guess why their voice has been restricted. No government should be allowed to silence lawful criticism through opaque processes. And no technology company should be permitted to hide consequential decisions behind unexplained notifications.

If the restrictions were justified, publish the reasons. If they were mistaken or unlawful, restore the affected rights. Let evidence decide—not political loyalty.

Watch and share the creator's account: https://t.co/nDn2eW2hgE

Now, @Muslim_ITCell is in the crosshairs.

Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

IFF statement on the geo-blocking of 26 Reddit posts in India

On 21 October 2026, Reddit, Inc filed with the Lumen Database a government takedown order from India covering 26 URLs and complied, so that all 26 posts are now geo-blocked in India (Lumen notice 100411498). The notice names neither a law nor an agency, since its “Laws/Regulations” field is blank and the request is attributed only to an “Agency”. The 26 posts sit in 18 subreddits, from r/Northeastindia to r/IndianDefense and r/myanmar, and were catalogued on 24 October by @geoblockedindia in a thread that also carries images of the notice.

Irrational censorship does not advance national interest

Nearly all of the blocked posts concern the India–China border. They include open-source verification of PLA footage from the June 2020 Galwan clash, satellite imagery reported by Indian newsrooms, a Caravan essay, a TRT World report on Beijing’s claim over Arunachal Pradesh, maps ranging from the one China draws to users’ sketches of proposed new states, and a question put to Chinese users. Several are five or six years old, and three had already been deleted by their authors.

IFF condemns this order as secret, disproportionate and unlawful. We do not dispute that the State may act against speech that genuinely endangers the defence of India, such as troop positions, operational plans, the identities of serving personnel or a hostile state’s coordinated information operation, and the twenty soldiers who died at Galwan deserve a country that takes its border seriously. Nothing on this list is of that kind, because every item was already public, whether released by the PLA, reported by Indian newsrooms or posted by ordinary users. Post 14 describes Indian soldiers holding off an armoured vehicle with sticks, stones and helmets, and their courage is not a secret, nor is there any reason to make it one.

Arunachal Pradesh is part of India and the country asserts that position with confidence, so it has no need to hide from its own citizens the map that Beijing draws, which they need to know in order to answer. Censoring Indian's discussion of the dispute does nothing to weaken China’s position and hands Chinese state media a ready story about Indian censorship. Two of the blocked posts, numbers 11 and 13, were themselves objecting to wrong maps, while others are users’ sketches of proposed new states. The secrecy surrounding the order protects no one but the official who signed it.

Whether this was a direction under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, or a notice under Section 79(3)(b) routed through the Sahyog portal, it fails the tests the Supreme Court has set. Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1 upheld Section 69A only because the 2009 Rules require written reasons, a hearing under Rule 8 and review under Rule 14, and none of these safeguards was observed here. A restriction must also be necessary and the least restrictive means available, and this order is neither, since blocking six-year-old threads answers no present danger, blocking posts already deleted shows that nobody examined the list, and blocking entire threads silences commenters nobody considered.

How Reddit works

Reddit is a federation of tens of thousands of communities known as subreddits, each created by users and run by unpaid volunteer moderators, while Reddit, Inc itself handles legal demands. Reddit says that content named in a government request is checked first against its own rules and then against local and international law, including human rights standards, before access is restricted in the requesting country, after which a reader in India sees a restriction notice while everyone else, including anyone in India using a VPN, still sees the post (Reddit Transparency Report, July–December 2025).

Because each post sits at a fixed URL with a threaded discussion beneath it, a block by URL hides the whole thread, including every reply beneath it, and r/Northeastindia has lost seven threads about its own borders for readers in India while a reader in Shanghai can still open them. The moderators who built these forums receive no notice and have no appeal, and the only public record of the order is the notice Reddit chose to send to Lumen.

Takedowns on Reddit are rising

India is now the second-largest source of the government takedown demands that Reddit receives. Between July and December 2025, Reddit received 169 such requests from 28 countries, of which India sent 21, second only to the UAE (Reddit Transparency Report, July–December 2025), up from fewer than ten in all of 2019. The demands have also grown bolder, as a 2025 order relayed through Pune Police named 825 posts about a matrimonial service and warned of a countrywide ban if Reddit did not comply, yet Reddit refused and the court agreed with it. Across all platforms, published analysis puts MeitY’s blocking orders at about 12,600 in 2024 and 24,300 in 2025. On 21 October 2026, Reddit complied with all 26 URLs without any public challenge.

Our demands

1. MeitY and the originating agency must publish the order, the provision invoked and the reasons for each URL.

2. The order must be withdrawn and access restored, and any post said to be unlawful must first go through notice and a hearing under Rule 8.

3. The Review Committee under Rule 14 must examine the order and publish its finding.

4. If the order came through the Sahyog portal, the Government must say so and stop using Section 79(3)(b) against speech while the courts decide its legality.

5. MeitY must disclose how many Reddit URLs it has had blocked since 2024, and on what grounds.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Indian founders running international companies, read this before your CA does 👇

US Inc, Delaware LLC, Singapore Pte, UK Ltd: setting it up online takes a day. Staying compliant in India is where most founders slip.

I put Claude Fable 5.1 on max effort for 1+ hour, digging through RBI, CBDT, Income Tax, GST and IRS rules, official sources only.

I'd missed 2 filings for 2 years myself 💀

Here's the full map 👇

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE MYTH
"If you run it from India, you must open an Indian office."

Not quite. POEM (Place of Effective Management) decides whether your foreign company is an Indian TAX RESIDENT. It doesn't force you to register an office.

And CBDT Circular 8/2017 keeps foreign companies with turnover ≤ ₹50 crore outside POEM.
https://t.co/vhIDHz1nlG

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT APPLIES FROM DAY 1, IN ANY COUNTRY, AT ANY REVENUE

① FEMA ODI (RBI)
An Indian resident owning shares of ANY foreign company = Overseas Direct Investment (FEMA Overseas Investment Rules 2022).
→ Form FC via your bank + a UIN
→ Annual Performance Report (APR) by 31 Dec every year
→ Investment within the LRS limit (USD 250k per year)
https://t.co/XAmuvMQiio

Missed it? Very common, and fixable:
→ Late Submission Fee: ₹7,500 + 0.025% × amount × years, ₹7,500 per missed APR (within 3 years)
https://t.co/vSjuKuintV
→ Beyond that: RBI compounding
https://t.co/FGYL787WdW

② Transfer pricing (Income Tax)
You own both the Indian and foreign company = "associated enterprises" (common holding ≥26%). Any payment between them = an international transaction:
→ must be at arm's length (a fair market price)
→ a CA files the report (Form 3CEB / Form 48 under the new Act). There's NO minimum amount
→ ₹1 lakh penalty if missed
https://t.co/nf5iY2wXF7
https://t.co/RMpSTQzx5a

③ Schedule FA (your ITR)
Your foreign company shares are a foreign asset. Disclose them every year.
Black Money Act penalty: ₹10 lakh per year. Since Oct 2024 it doesn't apply if non-immovable foreign assets total ≤ ₹20 lakh, but just file it.
https://t.co/M8ybGpDmS0

④ GST
Indian company → foreign company services = export of services (zero-rated), even between related companies (CBIC Circular 161/17/2021: "separate persons").
→ File a LUT every financial year
→ Keep the FIRA/e-FIRC for every inward payment
https://t.co/eVPPUZhaWn

⑤ PE: the one nobody mentions
Under India's tax treaties (e.g. India-US DTAA Article 5), a foreign company can have a "Permanent Establishment" in India if it's managed from here, or if services are performed here for a related enterprise. No ₹50 cr threshold.
https://t.co/ix9HhwopeJ

⑥ The foreign country's own filings
Every country has its own. The US example:
→ IRS Form 5472 every year for a foreign-owned US corp or single-member LLC. Miss it = $25,000 penalty
https://t.co/RUASzLnZvw
→ Federal return + state franchise tax / annual report
(Singapore, UK and UAE each have their own annual returns and filings.)

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE CLEAN STRUCTURE MOST FOUNDERS USE

🌍 Foreign company: customers, contracts, revenue
🇮🇳 Indian company: does the actual work, bills the foreign company cost + a fair margin
👤 You: director/employee of the Indian company, taking salary from India

Money comes in as export of services. The paperwork matches reality.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

✅ ODI: Form FC + UIN + APR (31 Dec)
✅ Transfer pricing report (3CEB) every year
✅ Schedule FA in your ITR
✅ GST LUT + FIRAs
✅ Real substance on both sides (avoid PE)
✅ The foreign country's own annual filings

Going Dark

The internet is going into a lockdown ....

Hundreds of millions of websites are potentially at risk from cyberattacks ...

Governments .. banks and major platforms have already taken their websites offline ...

Be prepared for something new ... It’s always followed by a crisis ....

W.H.G.

Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

A flaw called PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / 109619) - CVSS 9.2/10 CRITICAL - found in PHP itself, the engine that runs 70% of all websites. Found by AI, leaked Oct 20, patched Oct 21 at 6:40 PM PST.

HOW IT AFFECTS PAKISTAN:

National CERT (Pak-CERT) issued critical warning. 
They are auditing 300 government websites - 280 already done (93%). Found critical server misconfigurations and data leak risks.

Action: non-essential services shifted to read-only mode, WAF firewalls made mandatory. 
If you saw some .gov.pk portals slow or down on Oct 22-24, this was why. Not a hack, a defense.

2. Banks Are Already Under AI Attack
1Link - which processes 12 BILLION transactions / year (Rs 90 Trillion) for 42 banks, 1300 gov institutions - said it blocks THOUSANDS of attacks every month. 
Its CTO said last week: "AI agents are now trying to hack us too.

Most Pakistani e-commerce, WordPress, NADRA-linked portals, FBR, university sites run on PHP. 

If the host didn't update to PHP 8.2.35 / 8.3.36 / 8.4.27 / 8.5.12, an attacker can take over the server WITHOUT a password.

But if Pakistan's small businesses and hosting companies don't patch, the next attack will not be preventive.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

text:
Statement: Instagram censors a cartoon about censorship. IFF will challenge it.
A cartoon on comedy, copyright and the IT Rules has been withheld in India by an automated system that cites no order and gives no reasons.

On 27 October 2026, Instagram withheld in India a cartoon by Aadvik (@aaaaadvik ) who first published on 29 September 2026 as a collaborative post on the accounts of IFF, Aadvik and stand-up comedian Pulkit Mani. It shows a panicked man at a console in the image and style of the Prime Minister with red buttons marked "Censor", "Copyright" and "IT Rules", while a comic performs on a screen above him. Its caption reads, "Quick, check if comedy counts as a violation of copyright or a matter of national security." The post asked who decides what gets taken down, and on what grounds.

Instagram has now answered this literally by taking it down after close to a month. Its notice says access was restricted "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021. It names no order, authority, provision or ground. There was no prior notice and no chance to respond. The same cartoon remains available on IFF's X account. The post also carried an update on Pulkit Mani v. Meta Platforms Inc. & Ors., his Delhi High Court suit over fraudulent copyright strikes on his Instagram page, in which IFF appears for him pro bono. Meta, a defendant in that suit, has now hidden a post about it from Indian users in which it is the principal defendant.

In 1945, George Orwell wrote a preface to Animal Farm, a book four publishers had turned down. He noted, "the sinister fact about literary censorship in England," he observed, "is that it is largely voluntary." Unpopular ideas, he argued, could be silenced without any official ban, by institutions that guess what power wants and act first. The preface itself stayed unpublished until 1972 and in Nineteen Eighty-Four he gave this habit a machine, namely, the memory hole, a slot at the Ministry of Truth into which inconvenient records vanished, unexplained and beyond appeal. Today, the Ministry of Electronics and IT acts as this Ministry of Truth that covers up its gross incompetence in securing our cyber security by building an architecture of digital censorship that is implemented by technology platforms. It is under these IT Rules, 2021 that Instagram's "automated system" exists as a memory hole. It has swallowed a cartoon whose whole joke is a man reaching for the censor button without asking what comedy is. The absurdity Aadvik drew has now been actually demonstrated in stark reality.

This machine did not build itself and in April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts content flagged by government and police in India, and wants a fresh government direction before restoring anything later found lawful. MeitY's unpublished advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 pressed platforms, and Meta by name, for "enhanced diligence". The same notice has been served on cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account, on journalists covering the October protests, and days ago on comedian Kajol Srinivasan. The Union Government applies the pressure and Meta has chosen to answer it with a system that censors first and explains nothing.

IFF will soon challenge Meta's automated restriction system in an appropriate legal proceeding. A joke is not a threat to the nation, and we will not let Meta’s algorithms decide otherwise.

Our demands
1) Meta must restore the post in India, and tell IFF, Aadvik and Pulkit Mani which order, authority and provision it relied on, if any.
2) Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose the inputs on which its "automated system" acts.
3) MeitY must state whether any direction, Sahyog Portal intimation or advisory concerned this cartoon, and withdraw and publish its advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026.
4) The Union Government must restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or by intimations that comply with Rule 3(1)(d), and never by leaning on platforms.

Speak up
A memory hole works only as long as people accept it in silence. If you are a cartoonist, comic, creator or journalist whose post or account has been withheld with this notice, write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of every notice and we will try our best to provide you help pro-bono. Over the past 72 hours we have assisted close to 56 social media users, some of whom had their accounts restored. We are in this together!

text:
If a small law firm in India came to me tomorrow with zero leads from the internet, here's exactly what I'd do in the first 90 days.

One thing first. Bar Council of India rules ban advocates from advertising or asking for work.

So no "best divorce lawyer in Delhi" ads. No paid reviews. No "why we beat that firm" pages.

But the rules do let you have a website. It can show your name, contact details, enrolment number, qualifications and practice areas.

And nothing stops you from explaining the law in plain words.

That's the  plan. You don't sell. You answer the questions people type into Google and ChatGPT before they hire a lawyer. And your website drives people into a funnel and build trust.

DAYS 1–7: Fix the basics and find the questions

First, the Google Business Profile. Right name, office address, phone, hours, practice areas.

People search "lawyer near me" and "cheque bounce lawyer in Pune". Google shows the map results at the top. You want to be in them.

Then fix only what matters on the website:

• One page per practice area. Not one page listing 15 areas.
• Enrolment number, State Bar Council and qualifications on the About page.
• A disclaimer page. Most Indian firm sites have one.
• Phone and WhatsApp that work with one tap on a phone.
• One H1 on every page.
• Delete old blog posts that get no traffic.

I'm not chasing page speed scores. That's not why a firm gets no leads.

Next, find the questions.

Ask the partners to write down the 20 questions clients ask on the first call. These are gold.

Then find 3–5 sites that already rank for your kind of work in your city. Put each one into Ahrefs. Go to "Organic keywords" and set:

• Intent: Non-branded
• Lowest DR in top 5: up to 39
• KD: up to 25

Now you only see questions where weak sites rank at the top. If they can rank, so can you.

You'll get lists like:

• how to file mutual consent divorce in Pune
• cheque bounce notice time limit
• RERA complaint against builder in Maharashtra
• property share for daughters after father's death

DAYS 8–30: Build pages that answer the questions

Take every question. Google it. Look at the top 5 results.

Guides ranking? Write a guide. Firm practice-area pages ranking? Build a practice-area page.

Put the main phrase in the URL, page title, H1 and meta description.

Each practice-area page gets 600–800 words:

• What the matter is, in plain words
• The steps, in order
• The documents the client needs
• Which court or authority hears it
• How long it usually takes
• An FAQ
• Links to the related pages

The advocate checks every line. Wrong law on your own site is worse than no site.

Then add the top practice-area pages to the main menu.

For AI search, I'd type each client question into ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. Then look at the pages they cite.

For legal questions, it's almost always step-by-step guides.

So I'd open each one and note:

• How long it is
• Which questions it answers
• How it's laid out
• What it gets wrong or leaves out

Then write a better version on the firm's site, signed by the advocate.

Then write 5–10 articles under the advocate's name for legal blogs and news sites that publish practising lawyers.

Never pay to be featured. Paying for placement is advertising.

DAYS 31–90: Build trust

Get most links pointing to the homepage. Your bar association, your college alumni page, the articles you wrote. Homepage links lift every page on the site.

Publish one explainer a week. When the Supreme Court or a High Court changes the law in your area, explain what it means for ordinary people. In plain words. The same week.

Record each article as a 2-minute video. Google often shows videos for "how to" legal questions.

Let happy clients leave Google reviews. Never pay for them. Never write fake ones. Never trade a discount for one.

End every page with how to reach you. Phone, WhatsApp, address. No sales pitch.

That's it.

This is slow. Expect the first leads in a few months, not a few weeks.

But once it works, the person searching "what do I do after a cheque bounce notice" at 11 pm finds your page. Reads your name. And calls you in the morning.

If you run a small firm in India and want this set up, DM me. I have colleagues who do this every day.

Indian courts can assert jurisdiction over online defamation if the content is accessed and causes harm in India, as here (viewed at Adani's Kolkata office). They can issue injunctions enforceable against platforms operating in India, forcing takedowns. 

A final damages award is possible if liability is proved after full trial. Collecting it from a US resident is harder: any India assets could be attached, but US courts rarely enforce foreign defamation judgments under the SPEECH Act, which requires free-speech protections matching the First Amendment. Enforcement thus depends on assets location and international procedures.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

• Instagram: सबसे ज़्यादा लगभग 1 लाख (100,000) ब्लॉकिंग आदेश मिले।
• Facebook: करीब 80,000 टेकडाउन और ब्लॉकिंग निर्देश दिए गए。
• YouTube: लगभग 15,000 आदेश जारी किए गए।

प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी ने नई दिल्ली में आयोजित आठवें ब्लूमबर्ग न्यू इकोनॉमी फोरम (Bloomberg New Economy Forum) में देश के डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने विचार रखे।
उन्होंने भारत को 'लोकतंत्र की जननी' (Mother of Democracy) बताया और कहा कि भारत में 100 से अधिक भाषाएं, करीब 80,000 पंजीकृत समाचार पत्र और 1,000 से ज्यादा सैटेलाइट टीवी चैनल मौजूद हैं।
उन्होंने बताया कि भारत में 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग यूट्यूब और 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग इंस्टाग्राम का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो ऑनलाइन नागरिक चर्चाओं में सक्रिय रूप से भाग लेते हैं।
उन्होंने कहा कि इन डिजिटल मंचों ने एक ऐसा मंच तैयार किया है जहां नागरिक खुले तौर पर विचारों का आदान-प्रदान और राष्ट्रीय मुद्दों पर बहस करते हैं।

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

text:
https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu condemns arbitrary content and account restrictions faced by users on Meta platforms, X, and Reddit.

Over the past 20 days, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu’s Free Speech Tracker has recorded 200+ cases of content blocking and account restrictions on @Meta platforms, @X, and @Reddit. Many of the recently blocked posts were critical of the government, called for protests, featured journalists’ reporting, addressed ongoing issues, or even demanded justice in a murder case, among other topics. These restrictions are not only limited to feed posts, but Meta has also restricted Instagram Stories and comments online. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has also recorded various instances of FIRs filed against users raising their voices online.

Those affected include stand-up comedians, journalists, digital media organisations, civil society organisations, cartoonists, meme pages, political representatives and other users. Out of these, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has recorded 20+ independent journalists and digital media organisations who have faced restrictions, including @LiveLawIndia, @moliticsindia, and @4pmnews_network.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the platforms or through Meta’s automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight.

In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making.

These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI-generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless.

https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that these content and account restrictions are contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedowns, especially if done by automated systems. 

https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

The Election Commission has filed its reply in the Supreme Court to the petition on how the three-member Commission functions. 

27 pages, approved by all three members. Its argument: every decision was unanimous, and a Commissioner’s note is a “suggestion,” not a decision.

Here’s what it addresses, and what it doesn’t. 
🧵 (1/10)

2/10 – The notes Sandhu and Joshi who wrote the notes approved this affidavit, and it says all three SIR orders were passed unanimously. Under Section 18 of the 2023 Act, an objection on a file is not a decision of the Commission. When members disagree, the majority decides.

4/10 – Form 6 The Commission admitted the online version could be read as an amendment, said officers' steps needed correcting, and split the form back into two on Oct 21. That is the Commission fixing its own error before the court asked it to. The form's content, which links applicants to earlier rolls through their parents or grandparents, came out of the Bihar 2025 experience. The statutory form itself was never changed.

4/10 – ECINet If the expert committee follows Joshi's May 29 proposal, then the dissenting commissioner's view became Commission policy. That is the three-member system working as intended. It doesn't show that he was sidelined. The affidavit also confirms the ERO remains the legal authority over the roll, which was the concern behind the proposal.

5/10 – West Bengal The affidavit says the state CEO's officers filed the appeals under statutory guidelines and judicial instructions. Officers acting within their statutory role don't need the Commission's sign-off for each appeal. Each appeal goes before an appellate authority that decides it on its own merits, so similar grounds don't decide the outcome.

6/10 – Goa 88 of the 97 voters have already applied to get back on the roll through Form 6. The remedy is working for almost all of them. The software block in February is a fair question, but it was a technical failure, and the fix is now being handled by the IIT-IISc review.

7/10 – The July order The affidavit confirms that both commissioners objected and that the order was never implemented after their joint direction. Their check worked. A counter-affidavit answers the petition's legal claims. Naming or disciplining officers is outside its job.

An extract from an article by Avay Shukla relevent to today's judgement on Swatantra  Bhardwaj bail-
'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.
