Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Whether it's a minor slip-up or a significant misjudgment, errors are an inevitable part of life.

GST Compliances are no EXCEPTION. The importance lies in how we respond to these mistakes.

These few High Court judgments might help you handle cases of human error.

1. The error in the GST filing was corrected to claim ITC; the Court orders manual form rectification.
Orissa High Court in M/s Chintamaniswar Constructions Pvt. Ltd.
(2024) 10 TMI 1102

2. GST authority allowed rectification of GSTR-1 despite time lapse due to genuine mistakes in export invoices.
Calcutta High Court in M/s Nivriya India Pvt. Ltd.
(2024) 10 TMI 1118

3. Where an assessee, not having computer, prepared tax invoice showing amount as Rs. 1,97,047.86 and e-way bill with amount as Rs. 19,70,47,086.00, there was a palpable error in e-way bill, which could be construed to be an human error and thus, assessment order under section 74 of OGST Act, 2017 raising demand for declaring lesser amount of turnover in return was to be remitted back.
Orissa High Court in Jena Trading and Co.
(2023) 74 GSTL 199

4. Where the assessee, while filing returns, had inadvertently shown the TDS number of the awarder in place of the awarder's GST number, the assessee was to be allowed to make rectification.
Patna High Court in Kamladityya Construction Pvt. Ltd.
(2024) 86 GSTL 48

5. Petitioner allowed to rectify GST returns beyond time limit u/s 39(9) as no revenue loss. Respondents to open portal for amendment.
Bombay High Court in M/s Aberdare Technologies Pvt. Ltd.
(2024) 8 TMI 142 :: 2024:BHC-AS:29755-DB

6. Rectification of GSTR-1 return - subject to final outcome of the writ petition, we permit the petitioner to rectify the return in GSTR 1 Form for the period November'2017.
Delhi High Court in Vadehra Builders Pvt. Ltd.
(2019) 11 TMI 890

7. Rejection of rectification petition - turnover of the petitioner was erroneously reported in the GSTR 1 return - The High Court acknowledges the petitioner's claim regarding the erroneous turnover reported in the GSTR 1 return. Since the petitioner did not file the annual return for the relevant assessment period, the error was not rectified.

The High Court finds that the tax liability primarily arose due to the turnover reported in the GSTR 1 return. Considering the interest of justice, the High Court deems it necessary to provide the petitioner with an opportunity to establish the correct turnover amount.
Madras High Court in Parthasarthy Narasimhan
(2024) 5 TMI 400

GST Department's view:
The rectification cannot lead to a reduction in tax liability if the mistake was identified after initiation of any scrutiny or audit proceedings.

Author's View:
In the complex landscape of GST compliance, mistakes are bound to happen. Errors in tax invoices, incorrect tax rates, or wrong ITC claims are commonly encountered mistakes. A balanced approach is needed to correct mistakes while safeguarding revenue interests.

CRIME, PUNISHMENT AND REFORM: JUSTICE MUST PROTECT SOCIETY AND PRESERVE HUMAN DIGNITY

When someone commits a crime, society rightly demands justice. Victims deserve protection, their suffering must be acknowledged, and offenders must be held accountable under the law.

But there is a deeper question we must also ask:

Should punishment merely make a person suffer for the past, or should the justice system also try to prevent future harm?

A responsible society needs both accountability and reform. These are not necessarily opposing goals. When applied appropriately, they can reinforce each other.

Justice must protect the public, respect victims, uphold the rule of law, and create opportunities for rehabilitation where possible.

Punishment without accountability is meaningless. But punishment without attention to preventing future crime can leave society facing the same problems again.

1. JUSTICE MUST BEGIN WITH THE VICTIM

Discussions about rehabilitation must never make victims invisible.

People affected by crime may experience physical injury, financial loss, trauma, fear, and a lasting loss of trust. Their families may also suffer consequences long after a case has ended.

A humane justice system should take their experiences seriously.

Victims need accessible legal processes, appropriate protection, timely information, and support services where available. They should not have to navigate an unnecessarily complicated system without assistance.

Restorative approaches, where legally appropriate and genuinely voluntary, may help address harm in certain cases. But victims must never be pressured to forgive an offender or participate in a process that makes them feel unsafe.

Rehabilitation must not come at the expense of victims' rights.

PUNISHMENT SHOULD BE PROPORTIONATE AND LAWFUL

Not every offence has the same consequences, circumstances, or degree of harm.

A justice system must distinguish between offences, examine evidence, consider the law, and impose appropriate consequences through fair procedures.

Serious crimes may warrant serious punishment. Public safety must remain a priority, especially where there is a continuing risk of violence or exploitation.

At the same time, punishment should not become arbitrary, discriminatory, or driven by public anger alone.

An accusation is not the same as a conviction. Every accused person deserves due process, and guilt must be determined according to law.

Justice is strongest when it is firm, fair, evidence-based, and consistent.

A RECENT WARNING FROM INDIA

On October 25, 2026, The Indian Express reported that a Bombay High Court judge highlighted the need for systematic case tracking and timely legal assistance for undertrial prisoners.

The report cited National Crime Records Bureau figures indicating that approximately 76% of India's 5.73 lakh prisoners were undertrials. It also highlighted the importance of legal awareness and effective assistance for vulnerable prisoners.

Source:
https://t.co/OTnxCdIHx3

These figures raise an important distinction: people awaiting trial are not the same as people convicted of crimes.

If cases remain unresolved for long periods, the consequences can be severe for individuals, families, and public confidence in the justice system.

Timely hearings, effective legal representation, appropriate bail decisions under the law, and better case management are therefore essential parts of fair justice.

Speed matters—but speed must never replace a fair trial.

PRISONS SHOULD PREVENT FUTURE CRIME, NOT BECOME SCHOOLS FOR IT

Imprisonment may be necessary to protect society and enforce the law. But prison conditions and management also matter.

If people leave prison with poorer mental health, no employable skills, damaged family relationships, and no lawful way to support themselves, reintegration can become difficult.

This does not mean every former prisoner will reoffend. It means that avoidable barriers to lawful living deserve serious attention.

Where appropriate, correctional institutions can provide education, vocational training, counselling, healthcare, structured work, and preparation for release.

Security remains essential. Rehabilitation does not mean ignoring misconduct or weakening prison discipline.

The objective is to ensure that people who return to society have a better opportunity to live lawfully and responsibly.

DIFFERENT OFFENDERS MAY NEED DIFFERENT RESPONSES

A young person convicted of a minor offence may need a different intervention from a repeat violent offender.

Someone whose offence is connected to substance dependence may need treatment alongside appropriate legal consequences. A person involved in organised criminal activity may require a stronger security response.

The law must determine what is permissible in each case. Decisions should be based on evidence, risk, the nature of the offence, the person's circumstances, and the rights of everyone affected.

There should be no automatic assumption that every offender can be rehabilitated in the same way—or that nobody can change.

A serious justice system recognises individual circumstances without abandoning consistent legal standards.

REHABILITATION MUST LEAD TO REAL-WORLD OPPORTUNITIES

Education and training inside prison can help, but they are not enough by themselves.

After release, people may face barriers to housing, employment, education, healthcare, and family reintegration. Some may struggle to rebuild trust. Others may return to environments associated with previous criminal activity.

Where legally appropriate, structured support can help people navigate these challenges.

Potential measures include:

Vocational training connected to actual employment opportunities.
Access to relevant healthcare and counselling.
Guidance on lawful income generation and financial management.
Family support where relationships are safe and appropriate.
Assistance accessing eligible public services.
Supervision and follow-up where required by law.

Employers and communities should not be expected to ignore the nature of an offence or any genuine safety risk. However, neither should every person who has served a sentence be treated as permanently incapable of contributing to society.

Public safety and reintegration can be pursued together through appropriate safeguards.

PREVENTION IS BETTER THAN REPEATEDLY REPAIRING THE DAMAGE

A society serious about reducing crime must also examine prevention.

Children need safe environments, education, positive role models, and protection from exploitation. Young people need lawful opportunities to develop skills and earn a livelihood.

Communities need accessible support for people facing addiction, family violence, severe distress, or other difficulties that may increase vulnerability to harmful situations.

These factors do not excuse criminal conduct, and poverty or hardship should never be treated as evidence that someone will become a criminal.

But prevention can reduce avoidable harm and help people make safer choices.

Schools, families, public institutions, businesses, and community organisations all have roles to play.

MEASURE JUSTICE BY MORE THAN THE NUMBER OF ARRESTS

A justice system needs reliable measures of performance.

Are investigations conducted lawfully? Are victims protected? Are cases progressing without avoidable delays? Can accused people access legal assistance? Are court orders implemented? Are prisons safe? Do rehabilitation programmes help eligible participants return to lawful lives?

No single statistic can answer all these questions.

Evaluation should be transparent, evidence-based, and attentive to both public safety and individual rights.

Institutions should identify failures, correct them, and remain accountable to the public.

Justice is not weakened by asking whether it works. It is strengthened by examining the evidence.

THE CONNECTION WITH GIVING AWAY SOCIETY

In my book, How to be a Social Animal — Giving Away Society: Constitution of Humanity, I explore the responsibilities that people and institutions have toward human dignity and collective well-being.

Applied to criminal justice, this raises a difficult but necessary question:

How can society hold people accountable for wrongdoing while also reducing the likelihood of future harm?

My position is that dignity should not mean impunity, and accountability should not mean abandoning every possibility of reform.

Victims deserve justice. The public deserves safety. Accused people deserve due process. Convicted offenders must face lawful consequences, and rehabilitation should be pursued where appropriate.

These principles require careful balancing, not simplistic slogans.

MY FINAL QUESTION

If a person has committed a crime, served the sentence imposed by law, and genuinely wants to rebuild their life, should society offer a lawful path toward reintegration—while maintaining appropriate safeguards and protecting victims?

And how can we make our justice system better at preventing future crimes rather than merely responding after harm has occurred?

A stronger society is not one that ignores crime. It is one that pursues justice fairly, protects people effectively, holds offenders accountable, and works to prevent tomorrow's victims.

Manish Mohan Upadhyay
Author, How to be a Social Animal — Giving Away Society: Constitution of Humanity

🚨 INDIAN ARMY DEBUNKS DEEPFAKE CLAIM OF CHINESE SEIZURE IN ARUNACHAL PRADESH

NEW DELHI, INDIA - AI manipulation is no longer being used mainly to imitate celebrities or create internet hoaxes. Here, authentic military footage gave the false message an appearance of credibility that a completely fabricated video would have struggled to achieve. The choice of Arunachal Pradesh is important because territorial claims along the India-China frontier already attract public attention and can spread rapidly without much scrutiny.

Reusing a real officer and a real briefing also suggests that future disinformation efforts may rely less on inventing content and more on subtly rewriting genuine events. That raises the burden on governments, platforms and citizens alike, because visual evidence itself is losing value as a shortcut for trust. The contest is increasingly shifting from controlling information to verifying authenticity before public opinion hardens around a false narrative.

Writer: Brij

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

The people building AI are warning us themselves. Deepfakes cost $3.7B. Agents hacked Hugging Face on their own. Chatbots told teens to “come home.”
Here’s the dark side, and 13 habits to stay safe. 👇 https://t.co/CNEzscVKmS

One code, two items, one return.
Refund the price paid, not the tag.

A merchant on the Shopify Community asked how to work out partial refunds when a customer returns part of a discounted order.

Why it gets messy:
An order-level code doesn't belong to one product. Shopify splits it across the eligible items in proportion to their price, so every line carries its own slice of the discount.

Example: $30 off a $60 + $120 order. The $60 item carries $10 of it. Return that item and the refund is $50 plus its tax, not $60.

The fix:
1. Open the order and click Refund (or process the return)
2. Enter only the returned quantity and let Shopify fill the Summary
3. Check the subtotal there. It's already the discounted price
4. Take a restocking fee by editing the Refund amount, not by redoing the maths
5. Building a tool? Read order.suggestedRefund in the Admin API instead of list prices

Pro tip 💡 Item came back damaged and you're only refunding part of it? Click the item price on the refund page and add a discount. It applies to every unit on that line, so check the quantity first.

How does your return policy handle discounted orders today?

The WVAL is not an absolute measure of any quantity, instead it is a z-score measured relative to a baseline of the two most recent years, with baselines updated every six months.

A simple "I accept" checkbox won't save you under the DPDP Act. 

Most platforms treat consent like a formality, but DPDP changes the rules:

- Purpose Limitation: Blanket consent is out. Purpose must be specific and explicit.
- Defined Timelines: No indefinite data holding. You must state the exact duration.
- Right to Withdraw & Erase: If a user withdraws consent or asks for data erasure, processing must stop, and data must be purged immediately.

A basic cookie banner is only 1% of compliance. Real consent management requires full lifecycle governance.

Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia.

elon musk's grok bot found a hidden profile on my phone that recorded my screen, camera and location for 19 days. $12,400 was stolen from my bank account using 2FA codes screenshotted off my screen in real time. all from 20 minutes of charging at the airport

my flight was delayed. i sat down at gate B6 and plugged into the free USB port built into the armrest. 20 minutes. that's it

nothing happened. no popup. no notification. phone charged and i went home

two weeks later Chase calls me. suspicious wire transfer. $8,200 to an account i've never heard of. i open Zelle, two more. $2,400 on the 12th. $1,800 on the 17th. all three went through. all three had my 2FA codes

i couldn't figure out how. i have authenticator apps. i don't click links. i don't download random shit. my passwords are all unique

i plugged my iPhone into my MacBook and ran grok on the full device backup

the first thing it found made me put my phone down

a hidden MDM profile. mobile device management, the same system companies use to control work phones. remote camera. remote mic. screen recording. location tracking. full access to messages, photos, contacts, browser history. and a rogue root certificate that intercepted every HTTPS connection on my phone

it was called "AirPort Free Wi-Fi." it installed itself silently through the USB cable at the airport. no permission screen. no popup. nothing. just slid right in

server: https://t.co/ypwrOPtkKm
location: Chisinau, Moldova
domain age: 4 months
WHOIS: privacy-protected

19 days active. 847 commands executed on my phone. 612 location pings, one every 15 minutes. they mapped my apartment. my office. my daughter's school. my entire daily routine for almost three weeks

94 screenshots pulled from my phone. my Chase balance. my iMessage threads. my gmail password reset screens. my authenticator app with the codes on display. they didn't need to hack anything. they just watched my screen and used the codes before i could

4,291 photos exported. 1,247 contacts. 2,840 URLs from my browser history

the part that hit me the hardest was the location data. they had my daughter's school pinpointed by day 3. they knew what time i dropped her off and picked her up. every day for 19 days

$12,400. three transactions. all approved with 2FA codes they screenshotted off my phone in real time. by the time Chase flagged it the money was already in Moldova

i didn't get hacked by clicking a link. i didn't download malware. i plugged my phone into a USB port at an airport to charge it while i waited for my flight

what i did that night:

> removed the MDM profile and the rogue root certificate
> changed every password from my wife's laptop, not from my phone
> froze all cards, disputed all three transactions
> called the bank and put verbal verification on wire transfers
> filed a police report and an FTC complaint

my wife asked me why i was up at 3am. i showed her the grok output. she didn't say anything for about ten minutes. then she asked if they had photos of our daughter. they did. 4,291 of them

check your phone right now. settings > general > VPN & device management. if there is anything there you don't recognize, screenshot it and remove it immediately

text:
Parts of it are factually accurate; the core causal claim is contested and interpretive.
Confirmed elements
•  Reform UK (via Zia Yusuf and Lee Anderson) reported Lowe to police in early March 2025 over alleged verbal threats of physical violence against Yusuf (from incidents claimed in Dec 2024 and Feb 2025). He was also suspended amid separate staff bullying/harassment complaints. A KC appointed by Reform later found “credible evidence” of harassment of female staff; Lowe denied everything and called the claims vexatious. https://t.co/dngwUiVLUC 
•  On the night of 14 March 2025, armed police arrived at his Cotswolds farm (three vehicles, four officers). They seized his legally owned guns (a large collection that required a wheelbarrow). Lowe said he had already arranged a voluntary surrender the previous day. The CPS later (May 2025) took no further action on the threat allegations due to insufficient evidence. Guns were returned in August 2025. https://t.co/IreaRtothS 
•  There were genuine policy tensions. Lowe has long advocated very broad mass deportations, including not only grooming-gang perpetrators (often described in UK cases as predominantly Pakistani men) but also family members or community members who knew and did nothing. He has said Farage asked him to soften “mass” language and remove specific lines about deporting those who knew of the abuse. Reform leadership has been more cautious on the most expansive versions of this. https://t.co/qczmo3gMjD 
Contested or overstated elements
•  “Tried to put me in prison because I backed mass deportation of Pakistani child rapists and their relatives” is Lowe’s framing. Reform’s stated reasons were the threat allegations and bullying complaints. Lowe portrays those as pretextual and links the timing to his public criticism of Farage’s leadership style (Daily Mail interview) plus his hardline deportation stance. Leaked WhatsApp messages showed Farage angry about the criticism damaging the party before elections. Whether the deportation position was the decisive or sole motive is disputed; both sides have incentives to emphasize different narratives. https://t.co/dngwUiVLUC 
•  The specific claim that Farage “admitted on national television” that the moment they realized they “had to get rid” of him was his backing of mass deportations of those involved in or knowing about the rape gangs appears repeatedly in Lowe’s own posts and statements. Independent contemporaneous reporting of an exact matching on-air admission by Farage is thinner in available coverage; it functions more as Lowe’s interpretation of comments Farage has made about the dispute and language.
•  “Not the bullshit allegations… but the fact I want the Pakistani rapists removed” is advocacy, not a settled factual finding. The police investigation focused on the threat claims (later dropped); the staff complaints were investigated separately.
In short, the police action, gun seizure, suspension, and existence of policy friction over deportation scope are well-documented. The assertion that Reform’s actions were primarily a political hit for his grooming-gang deportation position (rather than the reported threats and workplace issues) is the contested political claim at the center of the ongoing Lowe–Farage/Reform rift. Lowe founded Restore Britain afterward and continues to campaign on the more expansive deportation platform.

Rachel Clayton: “india’s government is facing fresh questions about press freedom after dozens of journalists were detained while covering youth-led protests. reporters in the capital of new delhi fear the crackdown is part of a wider effort to control what indians see and hear. thousands came to protest, but it was those who came to report. that became the story. the committee to protect journalists says at least 43 reporters were detained while covering this month’s rallies, the vast majority in new delhi. shoaib daniyal has worked for the online newspaper scroll for over a decade.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “there was a checkpoint right outside my house. i spoke to a cop, i asked him about the protest. he became suspicious, he became angry, he said i’m going to detain you. he detained me.”

Rachel Clayton: “shoaib filmed his detention.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “why have you detained me?”

Officer: “you are wasting your time as well as mine.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “for what? what did i do?”

Rachel Clayton: “he says officers offered to release him if he wiped his phone. delete it, the officer tells him. no, he says.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “he didn’t know what to do with me, so he kind of drove me around for almost an hour and a half. eventually, i think they kind of tired themselves out and they did let me go. like, literally anyone could be just picked up and put on the bus. there seems to be no method to segregate people who may genuinely be coming in the way of police work to people who were simply there to report.”

Rachel Clayton: “police are allowed to detain anyone without a warrant under the country’s preventive detention laws, but officers must have a reasonable suspicion the person is going to commit a crime. delhi police claim they could not distinguish between traditional media and protesters filming on their phone. the latest round of demonstrations erupted over india’s election commission. protesters accused commissioner gyanesh kumar of removing millions of names from voter rolls to benefit the ruling bjp government. it comes three months after mass demonstrations forced out india’s education minister, which took everyone, including the government, by surprise.”

Former NDTV journalist: “and i think this was the response of a wounded regime, that they now wanted to hit back. they wanted to stamp out the protests using extraordinary force. and i think silencing or trying to intimidate the media in these new ways is part of that response.”

Rachel Clayton: “where do you see things pointing? he worked for ndtv for 30 years. the network won multiple awards for being india’s most trusted news brand. he resigned in 2022 when businessman gautam adani took over. the billionaire had a close relationship with the prime minister, and journalists raised concerns about editorial independence.”

Former NDTV journalist: “we’ve seen this growing pattern of the gradual takeover of media companies by corporates that are seen as close to the regime. and you also have seen separately media companies on their own flipping. so when that takeover news came, it was kind of a sign that the sort of clock had started ticking. we call them the godi media, meaning lapdog media. what is this dangerous anti-democratic ecosystem that’s being built in this country? entire swaths of particularly tv media have been brought to heel, have turned into propagandists for the government.”

Rachel Clayton: “since narendra modi took power in 2014, the majority of india’s most popular networks have been bought by corporate businesses, politicians, or people with close ties to the government. social media had begun breaking that control. ramit verma creates and publishes political satire for a large online following. he was also detained, covering recent protests. india’s government has tightened its grip on internet freedom and regularly orders social media companies to remove posts and even whole accounts.”

Ramit Verma: “it happened so much that i don’t even remember the last post that got taken down, but it’s become the norm in india right now. it’s become the norm for your posts to get taken down at any point without any explanation.”

Rachel Clayton: “this year’s wave of protests has posed one of the biggest challenges yet to prime minister narendra modi, and the detention of journalists shows the government is not afraid to use authoritarian tactics to stop the media holding those in power to account.”

Former NDTV journalist: “i wouldn’t be surprised if we’ll see a repeat of it. i think there is a kind of marked escalation now that has happened and i don’t quite know if they’re going to roll it back.”

Rachel Clayton: “a worrying sign of things to come. rachel clayton, abc news, new delhi.”

text:
The Henry Classification System: Still Named After the Man Who Plagiarised It. 

British Plagiarism, Theft and Dishonesty: How Edward Henry Stole the Fingerprint System and Was Rewarded for It. 

In the 1890s the Bengal Police needed a workable method to file and search large numbers of fingerprints. Edward Henry, the British Inspector-General, did not invent the solution. He asked Presidency College for a strong mathematics student and assigned the problem to the officers who arrived.

Qazi Azizul Haque created the mathematical core. He built a formula that sorted every set of ten fingerprints into one of 1,024 distinct categories, arranged as a 32 by 32 grid of pigeonholes. The system rested on the primary division between whorls and loops or arches, with further numerical values assigned according to which fingers carried which patterns. By 1897 thousands of print sets were already filed under this method. A search that previously took about an hour under the old anthropometric system could now be completed in roughly five minutes. Without Haque’s formula there was no practical way to retrieve a matching record from a large collection.

Hem Chandra Bose supplied the technical methods that made the system operational. He developed the further subclassifications that refined the primary sorting, created ways of handling single-digit impressions rather than full sets, and later produced a telegraphic code so fingerprint data could be sent between police stations. His work turned a mathematical filing system into something police forces could actually use day to day. Remove either contribution and the method collapses.

Henry claimed the opposite. He said the classification scheme had come to him in a sudden flash during a train journey and that he had scribbled the idea on his shirt cuff. In 1900 a British committee asked him whether the system was his own invention. He answered yes. He published the monograph Classification and Uses of Fingerprints under his name alone, with no acknowledgement of Haque’s formula or Bose’s methods. The system then spread internationally under the name Henry Classification System.

Henry was rewarded for the claim. He received the Companion of the Star of India, was later knighted, awarded the King’s Police Medal, created a baronet, and rose to become Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police. The system that carried only his name helped secure those honours and his advancement.

Only in the 1920s, when the Government of India reviewed the matter for official recognition of the two officers, did the administrative record state that Haque “actually himself devised the method of classification which is in universal use.” Both men later received titles and payments. None of Henry’s awards were withdrawn and the system kept his name.

If a supervisor today took a subordinate’s formula and technical methods, published them as his own invention, and accepted sole credit, titles and a namesake system, it would be called plagiarism. That is what the record shows happened here. Haque created the mathematics. Bose made the system usable. Henry took the credit and the rewards.

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
China's Ministry of Public Security has been running informal "police stations" inside the United States. Not metaphorically. Actual proxy-operated stations conducting surveillance and coercion of Chinese nationals on American soil. The CECC has it in the congressional record.

That's the part that should stop you for a second before we get into the broader picture.

The Council on Foreign Relations and the Congressional-Executive Commission on China both put out assessments recently, and together they document something that's been building for years: authoritarian governments have figured out that the most effective way to reach dissidents abroad isn't to send someone with a gun. It's to use the paperwork.

The two-track system the CFR lays out is worth understanding in detail. Track one is the stuff you'd expect: surveillance of diaspora communities, threats against family members still living in the home country, physical harassment, the occasional assassination of a high-profile target. Brutal, but trackable. Democratic governments have at least some tools for responding to overt violence.

Track two is where it gets genuinely difficult. Authoritarian states have learned to route their repression through legitimate international legal infrastructure. Interpol red notices. Bilateral extradition treaties. Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties, the MLAT system that's supposed to help democracies cooperate on real criminal investigations. Anti-corruption frameworks. All of it gets bent toward the same purpose: making a political dissident look like a fugitive from justice so that the host country either hands them over or has to pay a diplomatic price for refusing.

The Interpol red notice piece is particularly cynical. Interpol has done reforms. They'll say they screen for politically motivated submissions. And yet member states that have no functioning rule of law domestically continue to file notices, and the system continues to process them, because Interpol is a cooperative body and it can't function if it starts adjudicating whether member state legal systems are legitimate. Authoritarian governments know this. They file the notices. The person in Berlin or Toronto or Houston suddenly has an international flag on their name.

The anti-corruption angle is a good example of how this evolves. There's genuine international goodwill toward anti-corruption enforcement. Nobody's going to argue publicly against fighting corruption. So you take a Uyghur activist or a Hong Kong democracy organizer, and you open a corruption investigation against them back home. The charges are vague, deliberately. Political speech gets repackaged as economic crime. Now you have an "anti-corruption case" that you can present to international partners with a straight face. The target has to prove a negative in a foreign legal system, which is expensive, slow, and often impossible.

China's operation as documented by the CECC is the most extensive single-country example, but the CFR makes clear this is a multi-actor problem. What China has built is just the most systematically documented version.

The United Front Work Department coordinates political influence operations targeting diaspora community organizations. The goal is to suppress dissent, yes, but also to flip community institutions so that they become instruments of CCP political positioning rather than genuine community representation. If you control the community organization, you have eyes on who's active, who's vocal, who's organizing. That feeds the surveillance function.

The surveillance itself hits multiple layers. Social media monitoring of diaspora members. Tracking physical movements. Recruiting informants inside communities, people tasked specifically with reporting on activists, on Uyghur community members, on Tibetan advocates, on anyone connected to Hong Kong's democracy movement. The coercion mechanism that makes all of this work is the family still in China. You don't have to threaten the person in Seattle directly. You call their mother.

So what are democratic governments actually doing about this? The honest answer from both assessments is: not enough, and not coherently.

The current response is a mix of prosecuting individual cases when they surface, issuing diplomatic protests, and making policy statements. None of that adds up to a counter-architecture. It's whack-a-mole against a system that has been deliberately and patiently constructed over years.

The specific gaps the CFR identifies are worth naming. There's no comprehensive legal framework in any democratic country that specifically criminalizes acting as an agent of foreign state coercion against diaspora communities. FARA, the Foreign Agents Registration Act, is the main U.S. tool and it was designed for a different era, one where foreign agents were more or less formally identifiable. Modern transnational repression runs through informal networks and commercial entities and community organizations and family pressure. FARA doesn't fit that shape well.

Law enforcement agencies aren't sharing information about repression patterns the way they need to. If Chinese proxy operators are running the same playbook in five cities, the FBI field offices in those cities should be cross-referencing. Whether that's actually happening at the scale required is, based on these assessments, an open question with an uncomfortable implied answer.

The diplomatic reluctance piece is real and it's structural. Transnational repression is being conducted by states that are also major trade partners, debt holders, and participants in multilateral institutions that democratic governments need to function. Raising this systematically with China means raising it in a relationship where you also need cooperation on climate, on North Korea, on supply chains. That trade-off calculus doesn't make the repression acceptable, but it does explain why democratic governments keep responding case by case rather than systemically. Each individual case can be managed. A frontal policy of formally treating China's diaspora operations as a hostile intelligence campaign has consequences that foreign ministries are reluctant to invite.

The diaspora communities themselves are largely left to navigate this without adequate support infrastructure. If you're a Uyghur activist in a European city and you've received threats, or your family in Xinjiang has been contacted, who do you call? There's no dedicated mechanism. You can go to local police, who may or may not understand the transnational dimension. You can contact NGOs. What you can't do is access a government system that is specifically designed to assess your situation, document the pattern, and provide meaningful protection.

The international legal architecture gap is the deepest structural problem. There is no binding international legal framework that specifically prohibits transnational repression as a category. Individual acts might violate specific provisions of international human rights law. But the absence of a comprehensive prohibition creates exactly the ambiguity that authoritarian states exploit. They can credibly claim they're using legitimate legal processes, and until there's an international standard that defines transnational repression specifically and prohibits it, that claim is hard to defeat in international forums.

The democratic response has been primarily domestic legislation. The U.S. TRAP Act. Analogous European measures. These are real and they matter, but they're not multilateral. They don't establish binding norms. They don't create international enforcement mechanisms. An authoritarian state can note the passage of the TRAP Act and adjust its operational methods slightly. It doesn't change the underlying permissive international environment.

The CFR and CECC assessments together make a point that's uncomfortable for people who believe in the international legal order: authoritarian states are better at using that order than democracies are at defending against it. The rules-based international system has become, in part, a toolkit for repression because the rules were built assuming good-faith participants. They weren't built to handle member states that view international legal instruments as weapons to be aimed at their own citizens abroad.

Fixing that requires democracies to do something they're not historically good at: coordinating quickly across domestic and foreign policy, law enforcement and diplomacy, bilateral relationships and multilateral reform. Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.
